rc_b1:
Say clearly: "I am invoking my right to remain silent."

Then stop talking. You do NOT have to answer any questions — not your name, not where you came from, nothing. Anything you say CAN and WILL be used against you in court. Silence cannot be used as evidence of guilt.

This right applies: during a traffic stop · at your door · at the police station · after arrest.
rc_b2:
Say clearly: "I want a lawyer. I will not answer questions without a lawyer present."

Once you ask for a lawyer, police MUST stop questioning you immediately. Do not answer any more questions until your lawyer arrives — even if they say it will help you, even if they say the lawyer is on the way.

If you cannot afford a lawyer, one will be appointed for you at no cost. Ask: "I want a public defender."
rc_b3:
Say clearly: "I do not consent to a search."

Police CANNOT search your home without a warrant signed by a judge. They cannot search your car without probable cause or your consent. Your refusal cannot be used as probable cause.

If they search anyway: do not physically resist. Say "I do not consent" calmly and clearly. Challenge the illegal search in court — that is how suppression motions win.
rc_b4:
After arrest you have the right to be told what you are charged with. Ask: "What am I being charged with?"

You have the right to an arraignment — usually within 24 to 72 hours of arrest — where charges are formally read and bail is set. You have the right to enter a plea.
rc_b5:
You must provide: driver's license, registration, and proof of insurance.

You do NOT have to: answer questions about where you are going, consent to a search of your vehicle, or answer questions about whether you have been drinking.

Keep your hands visible. Move slowly. Say: "I do not consent to a search. Am I free to go?"
rc_b6:
Do not physically resist — even if the arrest is unlawful. Resisting adds new charges.

Do NOT: argue, run, reach into your clothing, make sudden movements, sign anything.

DO: stay calm, say "I am invoking my right to remain silent and I want a lawyer," remember badge numbers and officer names, call a lawyer or family member as soon as possible.
rc_b7:
At your bail hearing, the judge considers: severity of charges, criminal history, flight risk, and community ties.

You have the right to argue for lower bail. A bail bondsman can post the bail for you for a fee — ask the agent what they charge before you sign anything.

Open Justice Gavel → tap HELP NOW to find a bondsman and lawyer instantly.
rc_b8:
After arrest, ask to make a phone call. Most (not all) states allow this within a reasonable time after booking.

Use the call for:
• A criminal defense attorney
• A bail bondsman
• A trusted family member

Note: The right to a phone call varies by state. Some states have no statutory guarantee. If denied, document when you asked.
whn_dui_intro: A DUI arrest is serious but manageable. Here's exactly what happens — and what to do at each step.
whn_dui_1_what: Police pull you over, perform field sobriety tests, and take a breathalyzer reading. If you fail or refuse, you are arrested and handcuffed.
whn_dui_1_do3: Invoke your right to remain silent
whn_dui_1_dont3: Don't resist — even if you think it's wrong
whn_dui_1_tip: You have 10 days in most states to request a DMV hearing to fight license suspension — separate from the criminal case.
whn_dui_2_what: You are taken to the jail, photographed, fingerprinted, and your BAC is recorded. Your belongings are inventoried. You may be held until sober.
whn_dui_2_do2: If you are allowed a phone call, call family or a lawyer — and don't talk about the case on jail phones (they are recorded)
whn_dui_2_do3: Remember everything you can about the stop
whn_dui_2_dont1: Don't discuss your case with anyone in jail
whn_dui_2_dont3: Don't sign anything without a lawyer
whn_dui_2_tip: Jail calls are recorded. Say nothing about the arrest to anyone except your attorney.
whn_dui_3_what: Your first court appearance. The judge reads the charges and asks for your plea. Bail is set or reviewed.
whn_dui_3_do1: Plead NOT GUILTY at arraignment — your attorney may advise differently based on your specific facts
whn_dui_3_do2: Have an attorney present if possible
whn_dui_3_do3: Ask the judge to review bail if it's too high
whn_dui_3_dont1: Don't accept any plea without consulting your attorney first
whn_dui_3_dont3: Don't appear without understanding the charges
whn_dui_3_tip: Pleading not guilty preserves every option — reduced charge, diversion, dismissal, or trial. Your attorney will advise on the best approach.
whn_dui_4_what: The judge sets bail based on criminal history, flight risk, community ties, and charge severity. For DUI first offense, bail is typically $500–$5,000.
whn_dui_4_do1: Have a bail bondsman ready — ask what they charge before you sign
whn_dui_4_do2: Show community ties: job, family, address
whn_dui_4_do3: Let your attorney argue for lower bail
whn_dui_4_dont1: Don't agree to conditions you can't meet
whn_dui_4_dont2: Don't sign with a bondsman until they tell you the full fee in writing
whn_dui_4_tip: Use Justice Gavel → HELP NOW to find a bail bondsman near you in under 60 seconds.
whn_dui_5_what: Your attorney negotiates with the prosecutor. Most DUI cases resolve through plea deals before trial. Outcomes: reduced charge, dismissal, diversion, or trial.
whn_dui_5_do2: Enroll in a DUI program proactively
whn_dui_5_do3: Keep your attorney updated on any new developments
whn_dui_5_dont1: Don't miss a court date — it becomes a warrant
whn_dui_5_dont3: Don't discuss the case on social media
whn_dui_5_tip: First-offense DUI cases are frequently reduced or dismissed. An experienced DUI attorney can make a significant difference.
whn_drug_intro: Drug charges vary widely by substance and amount. Here's what the process looks like — and how to protect yourself.
whn_drug_1_what: Police arrest you based on probable cause — a search, informant tip, or traffic stop. The substance is seized as evidence.
whn_drug_1_do2: Say "I do not consent to a search"
whn_drug_1_do3: Invoke your right to remain silent immediately
whn_drug_1_tip: "I do not consent to this search" is not an admission. It preserves your 4th Amendment rights even if police search anyway.
whn_drug_2_what: Evidence is logged and sent for lab testing. You are booked, fingerprinted, and a bail amount is set based on charge severity.
whn_drug_2_do3: Note what police claim they found and where
whn_drug_2_dont1: Don't explain what the substance is
whn_drug_2_tip: Lab testing takes weeks. Charges may be reduced or dismissed if the substance tests differently than assumed.
whn_drug_3_what: You are formally charged. The distinction between possession and distribution determines severity.
whn_drug_3_do1: Plead NOT GUILTY at arraignment — your attorney may advise differently
whn_drug_3_do3: Understand the exact charge and potential penalties
whn_drug_3_dont1: Don't accept any deal without a lawyer
whn_drug_3_tip: Many states have first-offender diversion programs — complete treatment, charges are dismissed.
whn_drug_4_what: Bail is set. Possession charges typically carry lower bail ($500–$2,500) than distribution charges ($5,000+).
whn_drug_4_do2: Provide employment and family ties information
whn_drug_4_dont1: Don't agree to conditions that include drug testing if you cannot pass
whn_drug_4_tip: Tap HELP NOW in Justice Gavel to find a licensed bondsman near you immediately.
whn_drug_5_what: Your attorney will challenge the search, test the evidence, and negotiate a deal. Many drug possession cases result in probation, diversion, or reduced charges.
whn_drug_5_do1: Enroll in treatment proactively — it helps your case
whn_drug_5_dont1: Don't get re-arrested — it destroys your case
whn_drug_5_tip: After completing your sentence, many drug charges are eligible for expungement — use Justice Gavel to check.
whn_assault_intro: Assault charges range from misdemeanor to felony. The facts and your response in the first 48 hours matter enormously.
whn_assault_1_what: Police respond to a 911 call or witness report. If there is visible injury, arrest is often mandatory.
whn_assault_1_do2: Invoke the right to remain silent
whn_assault_1_do3: Do not discuss what happened with anyone at the scene
whn_assault_1_dont1: Don't explain your side to police
whn_assault_1_dont3: Don't post anything about the incident
whn_assault_1_tip: Anything you say at the scene will be in the police report and used against you in court.
whn_assault_2_what: Fingerprinted, photographed, charges entered. If domestic violence is involved, mandatory hold periods apply in many states.
whn_assault_2_do3: Note any injuries — or lack of them
whn_assault_2_dont1: Don't reach out to the other person
whn_assault_2_tip: If the alleged victim wants to drop charges, that decision belongs to the prosecutor — not the victim.
whn_assault_3_what: Charges are formally read. A no-contact order may be issued, preventing contact with the alleged victim.
whn_assault_3_do1: Plead NOT GUILTY at arraignment — your attorney may advise differently
whn_assault_3_do2: Comply immediately with any protective orders
whn_assault_3_do3: Get a lawyer before this hearing if possible
whn_assault_3_dont1: Don't violate a protective order — it is a separate crime
whn_assault_3_tip: Violating a protective order while your case is pending will result in additional charges and almost certainly destroy any deal.
whn_assault_4_what: For simple assault, bail is typically $500–$3,000. Aggravated assault with a weapon may be $10,000+.
whn_assault_4_do1: Have references from employer, family, community available
whn_assault_4_dont1: Don't try to negotiate bail yourself
whn_assault_4_tip: Find a bail bondsman using Justice Gavel HELP NOW — available 24/7.
whn_assault_5_what: Your attorney reviews evidence, witness statements, and 911 recordings. Self-defense claims are evaluated.
whn_assault_5_do1: Write down your recollection of events immediately — every detail
whn_assault_5_do2: Gather any witnesses on your behalf
whn_assault_5_dont2: Don't discuss the case on social media
whn_assault_5_tip: Misdemeanor assault charges are often resolvable through plea deals or diversion — a first-time offense rarely leads to jail time.
whn_gen_intro: No matter what you're charged with, the process follows the same path. Here's what to expect — and what to do at every step.
whn_gen_1_what: You are placed under arrest, handcuffed, and transported to the booking facility.
whn_gen_1_do3: Invoke your right to remain silent
whn_gen_1_tip: You have the right to remain silent. Use it. Say: "I am invoking my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer."
whn_gen_2_what: Fingerprinted, photographed. Personal items inventoried. Bail amount set or held for arraignment.
whn_gen_2_do2: Use your phone call for family or attorney
whn_gen_2_dont2: Don't sign anything without a lawyer
whn_gen_2_tip: Jail calls are recorded. Never discuss your case by phone.
whn_gen_3_what: First court appearance. Charges read. Plea entered. Bail reviewed.
whn_gen_3_do1: Plead NOT GUILTY at arraignment — your attorney may advise differently
whn_gen_3_dont1: Don't accept any plea without consulting your attorney first
whn_gen_3_tip: Ask your attorney about diversion programs — charges can be dismissed if you complete a program. Most people eligible for diversion never ask for it.
whn_gen_4_what: Judge sets the amount required to be released while your case is pending.
whn_gen_4_do1: Have a bondsman ready — they can post bail for a fee; ask what they charge
whn_gen_4_dont1: Don't agree to conditions you cannot meet
whn_gen_4_tip: Use Justice Gavel → HELP NOW to find a licensed bondsman 24/7.
whn_gen_5_what: Your attorney negotiates with the prosecutor. Most criminal cases resolve without trial.

x_court_forms_registry_federal_forms_pub: Federal forms are public domain. PACER (pacer.gov) required for e-filing in most districts.
x_court_forms_registry_fillable_pdfs_ava: Fillable PDFs available. AlaFile for attorneys only.
x_court_forms_registry_comprehensive_sel: Comprehensive self-help centre with plain-language guides.
x_court_forms_registry_arizona_has_regul: Arizona has a regulatory sandbox (ARS § 7-101) for legal tech. Set-aside (expungement equivalent) forms available.
x_court_forms_registry_judicial_council_: Judicial Council mandatory forms (JC forms) are the most comprehensive in the US. Fillable, saveable PDFs. CR-180 is the dismissal/expungement petition (PC § 1203.4).
x_court_forms_registry_connecticut_has_r: Connecticut has robust e-filing (JDP-CV-79). Criminal expungement called "erasure" in CT.
x_court_forms_registry_florida_supreme_c: Florida Supreme Court approved family forms extensively. Criminal pro se forms vary by circuit. Check local circuit court sites.
x_court_forms_registry_georgia_aoc_forms: Georgia AOC forms are limited. Most criminal forms must be obtained from individual county superior courts.
x_court_forms_registry_illinois_supreme_: Illinois Supreme Court Approved Forms (SCAP) — CR-401 Petition to Expunge and Seal. Robust e-filing via eFileIL.
x_court_forms_registry_ky_aoc_forms_sear: KY AOC forms searchable by case type. Criminal forms include expungement petition (AOC-491).
x_court_forms_registry_louisiana_uses_ci: Louisiana uses Civil Code (not Common Law). Criminal forms vary heavily by parish. Recommend Louisiana Civil Code § references in disclaimers.
x_court_forms_registry_maryland_has_one_: Maryland has one of the most user-friendly self-help portals. Expungement forms particularly well documented.
x_court_forms_registry_mass_gov_has_one: Mass.gov has one of the most navigable portals. Expungement forms for cases after Oct 2018 (MGL c. 276, § 100E–100U).
x_court_forms_registry_scao_approved_for: SCAO-approved forms. Michigan Clean Slate law (2021) expanded expungement eligibility significantly — forms updated to reflect.
x_court_forms_registry_guide_file_system: Guide & File system available for expungement — interactive interview-style form completion.
x_court_forms_registry_mississippi_forms: Mississippi forms are limited at state level. County circuit court clerks maintain most criminal forms.
x_court_forms_registry_nebraska_online_l: Nebraska Online Legal Self-Help Center is one of the better state portals.
x_court_forms_registry_new_jersey_has_ex: New Jersey has excellent self-help portal. Expungement form (A-2574) is fillable PDF with instructions.
x_court_forms_registry_new_york_courthel: New York CourtHelp is among the most comprehensive in the US. LawHelpNY.org is the LHI-powered companion.
x_court_forms_registry_nc_aoc_forms_well: NC AOC forms are well-organised by category. Expungement forms explicitly listed. Note: NC UPL laws are among the broadest — app must clearly stay in "legal information" lane.
x_court_forms_registry_oklahoma_forms_im: Oklahoma forms are image PDFs on OSCN. Oklahoma Legal Aid (oklahomalegalaid.org) has more accessible versions.
x_court_forms_registry_oregon_ecourt_pro: Oregon eCourt provides fillable PDFs and limited e-filing. Expungement called "Motion to Set Aside" in Oregon.
x_court_forms_registry_pennsylvania_crim: Pennsylvania "criminal expungement" and "clean slate" sealing have separate forms. PACFile for e-filing.
x_court_forms_registry_south_carolina_up: South Carolina UPL is a felony (S.C. Code § 40-5-310). Disclaimer language must be especially clear for SC users.
x_court_forms_registry_tennessee_aoc_pub: Tennessee AOC publishes fillable expungement petition (T.C.A. § 40-32-101). Criminal forms vary by General Sessions vs Circuit Court.
x_court_forms_registry_texas_law_help_te: Texas Law Help (texaslawhelp.org) is the official LHI-powered portal for interactive forms. Expunction (Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Art. 55) and sealing (Art. 55A) have separate processes.
x_court_forms_registry_utah_has_legal_te: Utah has a legal tech regulatory sandbox (S.B. 80, 2020) — one of the most permissive states for legal tech.
x_court_forms_registry_virginia_efileva_: Virginia eFileVA for circuit court. Expungement petition CC-1473.
x_court_forms_registry_washington_refers: Washington refers to expungement as "vacation of conviction" (RCW 9.96.060). The WA Courts forms portal is well-organised.
x_court_forms_registry_wisconsin_gf_form: Wisconsin GF-forms are official circuit court general forms.
x_court_forms_registry_d_c_superior_cour: D.C. Superior Court handles both criminal and civil matters. eFile DC available.

Justice Gavel is designed to help attorneys comply with professional responsibility obligations:

• ABA Model Rule 1.1 (Competence): AI-generated signals carry mandatory disclaimers. No output replaces attorney judgment.

• ABA Model Rule 1.6 (Confidentiality): We do not sell, share, or monetize client data. Zero third-party data sharing except as required for platform operation (hosting, AI inference).

• ABA Model Rule 5.3 (Non-lawyer supervision): All AI-generated content is advisory only and labeled as such. The attorney of record remains responsible for all legal advice.
x_attorney_privacy_data_at_rest_aes:

• Data in transit: TLS 1.3 minimum
• AI inference: Anthropic API (SOC 2 Type II certified)
• Payments: Stripe (PCI DSS Level 1)
• Infrastructure: Render (SOC 2 Type II)
• Database: Supabase on AWS (SOC 2 Type II)

No client data is used to train AI models. You may request complete deletion of your firm's data at any time by contacting privacy@justicegavel.app.
x_attorney_privacy_firms_requiring_forma:

x_ch_have_right_remain_silent: You have the right to remain silent -- use it. You have the right to an attorney -- ask for one immediately. If you cannot afford an attorney, one must be appointed for you. Do not answer any questions about the alleged offense until your attorney is present. Say only: 'I am invoking my right to remain silent and my right to an attorney.' Then stop talking.
x_ch_bail_money_paid_court: Bail is money paid to the court to secure release from jail before trial. The judge sets the amount at a bail hearing, usually within 24-72 hours of arrest. You can pay the full amount directly (gets returned after the case), or use a bail bondsman who posts it for a fee the agent sets — ask what they charge, and whether any of it is refundable, before you sign. If you cannot make bail, you stay in custody until trial or until the bail is reduced. Your attorney can file a motion to reduce bail.
x_ch_arraignment_first_formal_court: Arraignment is your first formal court appearance -- usually within 24-72 hours of arrest. The judge reads the charges, you enter a plea (not guilty is almost always the right plea at arraignment), and bail is set or reviewed. Keep it short: enter not guilty, say nothing else. Your attorney does the talking.
x_ch_have_constitutional_right_attorney: You have a constitutional right to an attorney. If you cannot afford one, the court will appoint a public defender at no cost. Request a public defender at arraignment. A public defender is a licensed attorney -- they handle thousands of these cases and know the local courts. Do not waive your right to an attorney.
x_ch_have_right_make_phone: You have the right to make a phone call after arrest. In most states this must be allowed within a reasonable time -- usually a few hours. Use it to call a family member or an attorney. Do not use it to discuss the facts of your case -- jail calls are recorded.
x_ch_police_can_search_without: Police can search you without a warrant if: you consent (never consent), you are being arrested (incident to arrest), they see evidence in plain view, there are exigent circumstances (emergency), or a warrant has been issued. Do not consent to any search. Say: 'I do not consent to a search.' If searched anyway, do not resist -- raise it with your attorney as a Fourth Amendment suppression issue.
x_ch_fifth_amendment_protects_from: The Fifth Amendment protects you from being forced to testify against yourself. You can invoke this right at any time -- before, during, or after arrest. Simply say: 'I am invoking my Fifth Amendment right to remain silent.' After that, answer no questions about the alleged offense. This includes questions that seem harmless. Silence cannot be used against you -- but anything you say can.
x_ch_expungement_seals_destroys_criminal: Expungement seals or destroys criminal records so they do not appear on background checks. Eligibility depends on your state, the charge, how much time has passed, and whether you completed your sentence. Most first-time non-violent misdemeanors are eligible after a waiting period. Use the Expungement Checker in this app for your specific state and charge type.
x_ch_dui_dwi_arrest_triggers: A DUI/DWI arrest triggers two separate proceedings: a criminal case and an administrative DMV hearing to suspend your license. The license suspension hearing has a short deadline -- usually 7-10 days after arrest -- and is separate from the criminal case. You need an attorney for both. Do not plead guilty at arraignment. Many DUI defenses involve the accuracy of the breathalyzer, the legality of the stop, and the field sobriety test procedure.
x_ch_domestic_violence_charges_often: Domestic violence charges often involve mandatory arrest policies -- police may be required to arrest even if the alleged victim does not want to press charges. The state, not the victim, prosecutes the case. Immigration consequences for non-citizens are severe. Bail may involve a protective order prohibiting contact. Do not contact the alleged victim, even if they want you to -- violating a protective order is a separate crime.
x_ch_drug_possession_charges_vary: Drug possession charges vary by substance, quantity, and whether the state considers it simple possession or possession with intent to distribute. First-time possession charges may qualify for diversion programs -- completing the program results in no conviction. Immigration consequences for non-citizens are severe even for minor drug offenses. Use the Diversion Checker in this app.
x_ch_felony_serious_crime_typically: A felony is a serious crime typically punishable by more than one year in prison (as opposed to a misdemeanor, which carries less than one year). Felony convictions have severe collateral consequences: loss of voting rights in many states, loss of the right to possess firearms, bars to public housing and some employment, and immigration consequences for non-citizens. Never plead guilty to a felony without fully understanding these consequences.
x_ch_misdemeanor_lesser_criminal_offense: A misdemeanor is a lesser criminal offense typically punishable by up to one year in jail (not prison). Class A or Class 1 misdemeanors are the most serious; Class C or Class 3 are the least serious. Even misdemeanors can have significant consequences for employment, housing, and immigration. Many misdemeanors are eligible for expungement after a waiting period.
x_ch_probable_cause_legal_standard: Probable cause is the legal standard police must meet before making an arrest or conducting a search. It means there is a reasonable basis to believe a crime has been committed. It is more than a hunch but less than certainty. If police arrested you or searched you without probable cause, your attorney can file a motion to suppress any evidence obtained as a result.
x_ch_plea_bargain_agreement_plead: A plea bargain is an agreement to plead guilty in exchange for a reduced charge or lighter sentence. Whether to accept depends on the strength of the evidence against you, the likely outcome at trial, and your personal circumstances. Never accept a plea without consulting an attorney who has reviewed the discovery. Once you plead guilty, it is very difficult to reverse.
x_ch_have_constitutional_right_jury: You have a constitutional right to a jury trial for any offense carrying more than six months in jail. A jury of 12 (or 6 in some states for misdemeanors) must unanimously agree you are guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. In a bench trial, a judge decides. Your attorney can advise which is more advantageous for your specific case and judge.
x_ch_discovery_process_through_which: Discovery is the process through which you get to see the evidence the prosecution plans to use against you. It includes police reports, witness statements, lab results, body camera footage, and anything the prosecution knows that might help your defense (Brady material). Your attorney files a motion for discovery. Under Brady v. Maryland, the prosecution must turn over any evidence favorable to the defense.
x_ch_sixth_amendment_guarantees_right: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the right to a speedy trial. Most states have specific speedy trial deadlines -- typically 70-180 days from arrest for felonies. Excessive delays can result in dismissal. If you are held in custody and your case is not being resolved, your attorney should file a motion asserting your speedy trial rights.
x_ch_bail_bondsman_posts_full: A bail bondsman posts the full bail with the court on your behalf in exchange for a fee the agent sets. Fees differ by agent and state, so ask what they charge, and whether any of it is refundable, before you sign. If you fail to appear, the bondsman is responsible for the full amount and may send a bounty hunter to find you.
x_ch_motion_suppress_asks_court: A motion to suppress asks the court to exclude evidence obtained in violation of your constitutional rights -- typically the Fourth Amendment (unlawful search), Fifth Amendment (coerced statement), or Sixth Amendment (interrogation after counsel invoked). If the motion is granted, the suppressed evidence cannot be used at trial. This often leads to reduced charges or dismissal.
x_ch_criminal_conviction_even_misdemeano: A criminal conviction -- even a misdemeanor -- can trigger deportation, inadmissibility, or loss of DACA status for non-citizens. Immigration consequences depend on the exact charge, not the name of the offense. Never plead guilty without having an immigration attorney review the immigration consequences. See the Immigration Consequences section of this app for detail by offense type.
x_ch_juvenile_court_separate_from: Juvenile court is separate from adult court and uses different terminology -- adjudicated delinquent, not convicted. Records are confidential in most states and can often be sealed automatically or by petition. A juvenile cannot waive Miranda rights in many states without a parent or attorney present. The most dangerous event is a transfer to adult court -- fight it immediately. See the Juvenile Justice section of this app.
x_ch_probation_supervision_instead_addit: Probation is supervision instead of (or in addition to) jail time, ordered at sentencing. Parole is early release from prison under supervision. Both involve conditions -- regular check-ins, drug testing, no new offenses, and often restrictions on travel and association. A violation can result in revocation and the underlying sentence being imposed. Attend every check-in. Communicate proactively with your officer.
x_ch_missing_court_date_results: Missing a court date results in a bench warrant for your arrest and often forfeiture of any bail paid. Appear at every court date. If you cannot appear due to a genuine emergency, your attorney must notify the court immediately and file a motion to continue. Do not simply not show up -- a bench warrant stays active until you are arrested or surrender.
x_ch_do_these_things_order: Do these things in order: 1) Say nothing except 'I want a lawyer.' 2) Do not resist -- comply physically while invoking rights verbally. 3) Remember the officer's name and badge number. 4) Use your phone call to contact family or an attorney. 5) Do not discuss the case with anyone in the jail -- conversations are monitored. 6) At arraignment, plead not guilty. 7) Find a criminal defense attorney before your next court date.

x_family_court_legal_custody_right_make: Legal custody is the right to make major decisions about a child's education, healthcare, and religion. Physical custody is where the child lives. Both can be sole (one parent) or joint (shared). Courts strongly prefer joint legal custody when both parents are fit -- sole legal custody requires evidence the other parent is unfit or unavailable.
x_family_court_every_state_uses_best: Every state uses "best interest of the child" as the standard. Courts consider: the child's relationship with each parent, each parent's ability to provide stability, the child's adjustment to home and school, any history of domestic violence or abuse, and in many states the child's own preference (usually considered at age 12-14). There is no presumption favoring mothers over fathers in any state.
x_family_court_criminal_record_does_not: A criminal record does not automatically disqualify a parent from custody. Courts look at the nature of the offense, how long ago it occurred, evidence of rehabilitation, and whether the offense involved violence or child endangerment. A domestic violence conviction is the most significant factor -- courts take it very seriously and may impose supervised visitation or limit contact. Drug offenses may trigger drug testing requirements. Non-violent, older offenses carry far less weight.
x_family_court_if_child_immediate_danger: If a child is in immediate danger, either parent can request an emergency custody order (ex parte order) -- a temporary order issued without the other parent present. The requesting parent must show immediate harm. Emergency orders are temporary and require a full hearing, usually within 14-21 days, where both parents can present their case.
x_family_court_once_custody_order_place: Once a custody order is in place, it can only be modified by showing a substantial change in circumstances -- a significant change in the child's needs or a parent's situation. Moving to a new state, a parent's incarceration, a significant change in the child's school or health needs, and evidence of abuse all qualify. Routine disagreements between parents do not.
x_family_court_have_right_represent_your: You have the right to represent yourself in family court (pro se). Many courthouses have self-help centers with forms and guidance. However, if the other parent has an attorney and the stakes involve custody of your children, getting at least a one-hour consultation with a family law attorney before your first hearing is strongly recommended. The decisions made in early hearings often set the pattern for years.
x_family_court_if_cannot_afford_attorney: If you cannot afford an attorney
x_family_court_legal_aid_organizations_p: Legal aid organizations provide free or low-cost family law help in every state. Income-qualified applicants can get full representation. Law school family law clinics also take cases. Domestic violence organizations often have staff attorneys for protective order cases. Call 211 from any phone to reach local legal aid referrals.
x_family_court_issued_by_police_scene: Issued by police on the scene -- usually the same night as an incident. Lasts 3-7 days. Requires no court hearing. If you have been assaulted or threatened and police respond, ask the officer for an EPO before they leave. This automatically gets you into court within a week for a longer order.
x_family_court_filed_at_courthouse_usual: Filed at the courthouse, usually the same day or next business day. A judge reviews your written declaration without the other person present (ex parte). If granted, the TRO typically lasts 20-25 days until the full hearing. You do not need a police report to file a TRO -- your sworn statement is sufficient.
x_family_court_issued_after_full_court: Issued after a full court hearing where both parties can present evidence. Despite the name, "permanent" usually means 1-5 years, renewable. The order can include: no contact provisions, stay-away distances, move-out orders (requiring abuser to leave shared home), custody and visitation terms, and firearm surrender requirements.
x_family_court_go_family_court_civil: Go to the family court or civil court clerk's office. Ask for the protective order packet. Fill out the petition describing specific incidents with dates, locations, and what was said or done. Be specific -- vague descriptions like "he was threatening" are weaker than "on [date] at [location] he said he would kill me and showed me a knife." File for free -- there is no filing fee for domestic violence protective orders in any state.
x_family_court_protective_order_can_prot: A protective order can protect you, your children, other family members, and even your pets. It can prohibit all contact (phone, text, email, through third parties), require the abuser to stay a specific distance from your home, workplace, and children's school, and require surrender of firearms. Violation of a protective order is a crime -- call 911 immediately if the order is violated.
x_family_court_if_have_criminal_record: If you have a criminal record
x_family_court_criminal_history_does_not: Your criminal history does not affect your right to obtain a protective order as a victim. Courts issue protective orders based on what the respondent did to you, not your history. However, if there are active custody proceedings, the protective order will affect custody and visitation arrangements.
x_family_court_national_domestic_violenc: National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233 (TTY: 1-800-787-3224). Text START to 88788. WomensLaw.org has state-specific protective order information for all 50 states. Law enforcement, hospitals, and domestic violence shelters can all help connect you to emergency protective order processes.
x_family_court_every_state_uses_formula: Every state uses a formula. Most states use an income shares model -- both parents' incomes are combined, the total child support obligation is calculated based on the combined income and number of children, then each parent pays their proportional share. The parent who pays child support (the non-custodial parent) typically pays their share to the other parent. Calculators are available on every state's family court website.
x_family_court_if_unemployed_underemploy: If you are unemployed or underemployed, courts will often impute income -- calculate support based on what you could earn, not what you currently earn. This is based on your work history, education, and local job market. If you are genuinely unable to work due to incarceration, disability, or documented job loss, this can be presented. Self-employed income is harder to hide than many believe -- courts look at tax returns, bank statements, and lifestyle.
x_family_court_if_incarcerated_still_leg: If you are incarcerated, you are still legally obligated to pay child support unless you petition the court for a modification. Arrears (unpaid support) accumulate during incarceration in most states. Some states automatically suspend support during incarceration -- most do not. File a modification petition immediately upon incarceration. The court can set a nominal amount ($0 or minimal) until release. Failure to do this results in large arrears that are very difficult to discharge.
x_family_court_child_support_can_be: Child support can be modified when there is a substantial change in circumstances -- typically a 15-25% change in income, a significant change in the child's needs, or a change in custody arrangement. Either parent can request a modification. File promptly -- modifications are rarely retroactive. If you lose your job, file for modification the same week, not months later.
x_family_court_unpaid_child_support_trea: Unpaid child support is treated very seriously. Consequences include: driver's license suspension, professional license suspension, passport denial, tax refund interception, bank account levy, wage garnishment, and ultimately contempt of court which can result in jail. None of these consequences are suspended during a pending modification -- file the modification first.
x_family_court_every_state_has_child: Every state has a Child Support Enforcement (CSE) agency -- free service that helps establish, enforce, and modify support orders. If you are the custodial parent trying to collect, contact your state's CSE agency. If you are the paying parent who needs a modification, consult a family law attorney or your county's self-help center.
x_family_court_this_information_general_: This information is for general education only and is not legal advice. Laws vary by state. Consult a licensed attorney for advice about your situation.

x_housing_rights_hud_fair_housing_act: HUD and the Fair Housing Act
x_housing_rights_department_housing_urba: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) issued guidance in 2016 stating that blanket policies refusing housing to people with criminal records may violate the Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. § 3604) because they have a disparate impact on protected classes -- particularly Black and Hispanic Americans. Landlords and housing providers must conduct an individualized assessment, not automatic rejection based on a record.
x_housing_rights_what_landlords_can_cann: What landlords can and cannot do
x_housing_rights_landlords_can_consider_:
Landlords CAN: consider criminal history as one factor, use a policy that excludes people convicted of manufacturing or distributing controlled substances, and deny housing when the individual poses a demonstrable risk to others or property.

Landlords CANNOT: automatically deny everyone with any criminal history, use criminal history as a pretext for race discrimination, or apply policies that have a disparate impact without a legitimate justification. A single arrest without conviction cannot be used as a basis for denial.
x_housing_rights_fair_chance_housing_sta: Fair Chance Housing -- state and local laws
x_housing_rights_growing_number_cities_s: Growing number of cities and states have enacted "Fair Chance Housing" laws that limit when and how criminal history can be used in housing decisions. These laws typically: prohibit asking about criminal history before a conditional offer is made (similar to ban-the-box in employment), require individualized assessment, and limit the lookback period for convictions. Cities with strong Fair Chance Housing laws include Seattle, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Washington DC. Check your city or county's housing authority website for local rules.
x_housing_rights_public_housing_authorit:
Public housing authorities (PHAs) have specific federal rules. Certain convictions are mandatory bars to public housing: lifetime sex offender registration, methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted housing. All other criminal history is subject to PHA discretion. PHAs must use an individualized assessment and consider factors like: age at time of offense, nature and severity, evidence of rehabilitation, time elapsed, and whether the person poses a current risk.

Section 8 (Housing Choice Vouchers) follows the same rules as public housing.
x_housing_rights_if_denied_housing_based:
If you are denied housing based on criminal history:
1. Request a written explanation -- you have the right to know the specific reason.
2. Request an individualized assessment if one was not conducted.
3. Gather evidence of rehabilitation: employment, education, family ties, community ties, letters from counselors or employers.
4. File a complaint with HUD if you believe the denial was discriminatory: hud.gov/program_offices/fair_housing_equal_opp.
5. Contact a local fair housing organization -- most provide free advocacy.
x_housing_rights_sealed_expunged_record_: A sealed or expunged record generally cannot be used in housing decisions. After sealing, you typically do not have to disclose the offense on rental applications. However, some housing providers -- particularly federally subsidized housing -- may have access to FBI records that reflect arrests even after state-level sealing. Private landlords running standard background checks generally see only state records, which reflect sealed records as sealed.
x_housing_rights_national_fair_housing_a: National Fair Housing Alliance: nationalfairhousing.org. HUD Housing Discrimination Complaint: hud.gov. NLIHC (National Low Income Housing Coalition): nlihc.org. Reentry housing resources by state: reentrycouncil.org. Call 211 for local emergency housing assistance.
x_housing_rights_pay_quit_have_x: Pay or Quit: you have X days to pay overdue rent or vacate. Cure or Quit: you have X days to fix a lease violation or vacate. Unconditional Quit: you must vacate with no option to fix (usually reserved for serious violations or repeated offenses). The clock starts when you receive the notice -- count carefully.
x_housing_rights_moment_receive_eviction: The moment you receive an eviction notice, your clock starts. Typical timelines: Pay or Quit notices give 3-5 days in most states. After the notice period, the landlord files an eviction lawsuit. After filing, you have a set time to respond (often 5-10 days). The hearing is usually 2-4 weeks after filing. A default judgment is entered if you don't respond or appear. A writ of possession allows physical removal -- usually 5-14 days after judgment.
x_housing_rights_rights_eviction_proceed: Your rights in an eviction proceeding
x_housing_rights_have_right_appear_court: You have the right to appear in court and contest the eviction. You have the right to raise defenses: the landlord did not follow proper notice procedures, the unit is uninhabitable (warranty of habitability), the eviction is retaliation for complaining about conditions, the landlord accepted rent after the notice (waiving the notice), or the eviction is discriminatory. You have the right to request a jury trial in most states. You do not have to leave until a court orders it and a sheriff or marshal executes the writ.
x_housing_rights_landlord_cannot_lock_ou: A landlord cannot lock you out, remove your belongings, shut off utilities, or remove doors or windows to force you to leave. These actions are illegal in every state regardless of whether you owe rent. If a landlord does any of these, call the police and consult a tenant rights attorney immediately. You may be entitled to damages.
x_housing_rights_emergency_rental_assist: Emergency rental assistance (ERA) programs exist in most states and counties -- funded federally but administered locally. These programs can pay overdue rent directly to the landlord and stop an eviction. Apply immediately if you are behind on rent -- do not wait for an eviction notice. Find programs at: consumerfinance.gov/renthelp. Many programs also require the landlord to participate -- landlords must accept ERA funds in most jurisdictions with ERA programs.
x_housing_rights_eviction_judgment_appea: An eviction judgment appears on your rental history for 7 years and is visible to landlords on screening reports. This makes finding new housing very difficult. Options: seek housing through organizations that work with people who have eviction histories, look for private landlords who do their own screening rather than using third-party services, apply for public housing (PHAs must do individualized assessment), and work with a housing counselor (free through HUD-approved agencies: hud.gov/housingcounseling).
x_immigration_consequences_broadest_most: The broadest and most severe category. Includes murder, drug trafficking, crimes of violence with 1+ yr sentence, theft/fraud with 1+ yr, sexual abuse of a minor, and many others.
x_immigration_consequences_any_drug_conv: Any drug conviction -- including misdemeanor possession -- makes a non-citizen deportable. Exception: a single offense of simple possession of 30g or less of marijuana may qualify for a discretionary waiver. Drug trafficking is an aggravated felony.
x_immigration_consequences_conviction_do: Conviction for domestic violence, stalking, child abuse, child neglect, or violation of a protective order makes a non-citizen deportable. This includes misdemeanor domestic battery in many jurisdictions.
x_immigration_consequences_any_convictio: Any conviction relating to purchase, sale, or possession of a firearm or destructive device triggers deportability.
x_immigration_consequences_two_more_crim: Two or more crimes involving moral turpitude (CIMT)
x_immigration_consequences_crimes_involv: Crimes involving fraud, theft, or intentional harm to persons or property. Two or more CIMTs at any time after entry, or one CIMT within 5 years of entry with potential sentence of 1+ year, triggers deportability.
x_immigration_consequences_inadmissibili: Inadmissibility -- bars re-entry or status change
x_immigration_consequences_one_cimt_with: One CIMT with potential sentence of 1+ year makes a non-citizen inadmissible (bars adjustment of status, re-entry, naturalization). The "petty offense exception" may apply for sentences under 6 months for offenses carrying max 1 year.
x_immigration_consequences_any_drug_offe: Any drug offense conviction or admission
x_immigration_consequences_conviction_ev: A conviction or even an admission to a drug offense to an immigration officer makes someone inadmissible. This includes marijuana offenses legal in the state where they occurred -- federal law controls immigration consequences.
x_immigration_consequences_conviction_ad: Conviction or admission to engaging in prostitution within 10 years of visa or adjustment application.
x_immigration_consequences_not_criminal_: Not a criminal matter, but relevant context: communicable disease, lack of required vaccinations, or mental disorder with harmful behavior can independently bar admission.
x_immigration_consequences_less_severe_b: Other offenses to review with a lawyer
x_immigration_consequences_may_may_not_b: May or may not be a CIMT depending on the specific statute and jurisdiction. Must be analyzed case-by-case. Some simple assault convictions are not deportable -- an immigration attorney must review.
x_immigration_consequences_not_automatic: Not automatically a CIMT. However, DUI combined with other facts (prior convictions, aggravating circumstances, underlying drug charge) can trigger consequences. A DUI may also affect naturalization by evidence of bad moral character. Must be reviewed individually.
x_immigration_consequences_shoplifting_w: Shoplifting with conviction may be a CIMT depending on the value of the property and state law. Items worth $500+ are more likely to qualify. Items worth less, especially with no prior criminal history, often do not.
x_immigration_consequences_generally_not: Generally not a CIMT. However, "fighting words" or assault-based disorderly conduct statutes may qualify. Review the specific elements of conviction.
x_immigration_consequences_daca_does_not: DACA does not provide a path to permanent status and offers no protection against deportation for significant criminal offenses. DACA termination is automatic for conviction of a felony, a significant misdemeanor (as defined by DHS -- includes domestic violence, sexual abuse, burglary, DUI, unlawful possession of a firearm, and drug offenses), or three or more misdemeanors. A DACA recipient arrested for any offense should consult an immigration attorney immediately -- before any plea is entered.
x_immigration_consequences_lawful_perman: Lawful permanent residents can be deported. Deportation is not automatic for most offenses -- it requires a removal proceeding before an immigration judge. Green card holders should NEVER plead guilty to any offense -- even a misdemeanor -- without consulting an immigration attorney, because the immigration consequences of a "minor" state crime can include permanent deportation.
x_immigration_consequences_any_criminal_: Any criminal conviction can result in visa revocation, denial of visa renewal, or denial of re-entry. The State Department can revoke a visa immediately upon notification of a conviction. A visa holder who travels outside the US after a conviction may be denied re-entry. Non-immigrant visa holders have the fewest protections of any immigration status.
x_immigration_consequences_naturalize_ap: To naturalize, an applicant must demonstrate "good moral character" for the 5 years before filing (3 years for married-to-citizen applicants). Any criminal conviction in that period is potentially disqualifying. Multiple misdemeanors, DUI, and offenses involving fraud or moral turpitude can also bar naturalization. Applicants with any criminal history should consult an immigration attorney before filing.
x_immigration_consequences_padilla_warni: Padilla warnings -- what your criminal attorney owes you
x_immigration_consequences_under_padilla: Under Padilla v. Kentucky (2010), the Supreme Court held that criminal defense attorneys must advise non-citizen clients about the immigration consequences of a plea. If your attorney did not warn you about immigration consequences before you pleaded guilty, you may have a claim for ineffective assistance of counsel. This can be grounds to vacate the conviction. Consult both a criminal defense attorney and an immigration attorney immediately.
x_immigration_consequences_if_were_convi: If you were convicted without Padilla warnings, or if new law changes the immigration consequences of your conviction, it may be possible to vacate the conviction through post-conviction relief. This is complex, jurisdiction-specific, and time-sensitive. An immigration attorney and a post-conviction specialist must work together. In some states, specialized clinics handle immigration-related vacaturs.
x_immigration_consequences_national_immi: National Immigration Project: nipnlg.org. Immigrant Defense Project: immigrantdefenseproject.org. CLINIC (Catholic Legal Immigration Network): cliniclegal.org. ILRC (Immigrant Legal Resource Center): ilrc.org. Call 211 for local immigration legal aid referrals.
x_interrogation_recorder_recording_conse: Recording-consent law depends on the state you are in right now. Justice Gavel checks your location once to show the right warning before you record.

x_juvenile_justice_juvenile_can_be_taken: A juvenile can be taken into custody by police for a delinquent act (crime) or status offense (truancy, curfew, running away). Police must notify parents or guardians promptly -- usually within a few hours.

x_juvenile_justice_if_juvenile_held_dete: If the juvenile is held in detention (juvenile hall), a detention hearing must happen quickly -- usually within 24 to 72 hours. The judge decides whether detention continues or the juvenile is released to parents.
x_juvenile_justice_right_attorney_applie: The right to an attorney applies at the detention hearing. This is In re Gault (1967) -- the Supreme Court established that juveniles have due process rights in juvenile court. Bail is not typically used in juvenile court; release is to parental custody.
x_juvenile_justice_detention_hearing_fir: The detention hearing is the first opportunity for an attorney to argue for release. A prepared attorney who knows the family situation significantly increases the odds of release.
x_juvenile_justice_prosecutor_some_state: The prosecutor (or in some states the probation department) files a petition alleging the juvenile is delinquent. x_juvenile_justice_juvenile_has_right_de: The juvenile has the right to deny the petition and contest it at an adjudicatory hearing. No jury trial in most states -- a judge decides.
x_juvenile_justice_language_different_ju: The language is different. The juvenile is not "convicted" -- they are "adjudicated delinquent." This distinction matters enormously for record sealing.
x_juvenile_justice_this_juvenile_equival: This is the juvenile equivalent of a trial. A judge (not a jury in most states) hears evidence and decides whether the juvenile committed the alleged offense. The standard is still "beyond a reasonable doubt."
x_juvenile_justice_full_due_process_righ: Full due process rights apply: right to notice of charges, right to an attorney, right to confront and cross-examine witnesses, right against self-incrimination. Established by In re Gault, 387 U.S. 1 (1967).

x_juvenile_justice_disposition_where_att: Disposition is where the attorney's work matters most. Community ties, school performance, family support, and demonstrated remorse all influence the outcome. A good attorney presents all of it.

iced_r1_body:
You do NOT have to answer questions about where you were born, how you entered the US, or your immigration status.

Say exactly: "I am exercising my right to remain silent."
iced_r2_body:
You can stay silent and say you want to talk to a lawyer before answering questions. In immigration proceedings you have the right to a lawyer, but the government does not provide one for free — the free legal service providers below may help. Ask to make a phone call.

Say: "I want to remain silent. I want to speak with a lawyer."
iced_r3_body: Never sign documents ICE gives you without a lawyer. This includes "voluntary departure" forms. Signing can permanently waive your right to a hearing before a judge.
iced_r4_body: ICE cannot enter your home without a judicial warrant signed by a JUDGE — not an ICE "administrative warrant." Ask them to slide it under the door. If they cannot, do not open the door. You may speak through the closed door.
iced_r5_body: These rights apply to every person in the United States — citizen, green card holder, visa holder, DACA recipient, undocumented person, or asylum seeker. Your immigration status does NOT change these rights.
iced_step_1: Stay calm. Panic leads to mistakes. Breathe.
iced_step_2: Say only: "I want a lawyer. I am exercising my right to remain silent." Then stop talking.
iced_step_3: Do NOT run, resist physically, or argue with officers.
iced_step_4: Write down or memorize: officer name, badge number, agency, and vehicle number.
iced_step_5: Call — or have a family member call — an immigration attorney or legal aid immediately.
iced_step_6: If released, write down everything that happened as soon as possible.

fa_plans_partner: Only a partner or firm admin can ask about plans.
fa_signin_body: Sign in with your attorney account to start or manage a firm workspace.
fa_trial_terms: Free for {days} days with up to {seats} seats. No card needed.
pay_confirm_retry: Your payment may have gone through, but we couldn't confirm it yet. Try again in a moment; you won't be charged twice.
pay_failed: Payment couldn't be started. Try again.
pay_offline: You're offline. Check your connection and try again.
plan_bondsman_leads_note: Leads are bought one at a time for a flat {fee} each, with or without a plan.
plan_cancel_body: Your plan stays active until the end of the period you've paid for, then it won't renew.
plan_footer_card: A card is needed to start. If the plan has a free trial, you're charged when it ends unless you cancel first.
plan_free_chat: AI legal chat, with a daily limit
plan_intro_consumer: These are free for everyone. A plan adds more.
plan_intro_pro: Plans for attorneys and bail agents.
plan_status_past_due: Payment failed. Update your card to keep your plan.
plan_switch_body: The price difference for the rest of this period is charged or credited right away.
st_conflicts_hint: Check names against your firm's matters
sos_btn_hint: Tap, then confirm to send your alert. Nothing is sent until you confirm.
legal_unverified_withheld: We haven't checked these rules for {state} against the official law yet, so we don't show them. Wrong legal numbers can hurt you. A criminal defense lawyer or public defender in {state} can tell you the current rule.
legal_verified_source_line: Checked against {source} on {date}. Not reviewed by a lawyer.
x_interrogation_recorder_mixed_consent_s: Mixed rules: some recordings here need everyone's consent
x_recovery_agents_secondary_source: Checked against a 50-state summary, not the statute itself. Confirm with your state Department of Insurance before any apprehension.
cdd_sms_consent: By turning on text reminders, you agree to receive automated court-date reminder texts from Justice Gavel at this number (up to 4 per court date). Consent is not required to use the app. Msg & data rates may apply. Reply STOP to cancel, HELP for help. See our Terms and Privacy Policy.
ckm_included: Check-ins and court reminders are included in every bail-agent plan. No per-defendant fee.
bdk_intro: Your bonds, paperwork, payments, powers and reports in one place.
bdk_dashboard_teaser: Bonds, paperwork with e-signature, payments and receipts, power inventory and surety reports — included in your plan.
bdk_sign_in_body: Sign in with your bail-agent account to use the Bond Desk.
bdk_no_plan_body: The Bond Desk is included in every bail-agent plan. Choose a plan to start.
bdk_not_agent_body: The Bond Desk is the office tool for licensed bail agents: bond records, paperwork to sign, payments and reports. Set up your bail-agent profile on the lead dashboard first.
bdk_load_failed: Could not load. Check your connection and pull down to try again.
bdk_save_failed: Could not save. Please try again.
bdk_texts_off: Texting is not set up on this server yet, so links and reminders go by e-mail, or you can copy the link and send it yourself.
bdk_err_amount: Enter an amount in dollars, like 1500 or 1500.50.
bdk_err_state: Use the 2-letter state code, like TN.
bdk_err_email: That e-mail address does not look right.
bdk_err_deadline: Enter the forfeiture deadline as YYYY-MM-DD.
bdk_err_pay_date: Enter the date it was received (YYYY-MM-DD, not in the future).
bdk_err_over_balance: That is more than the balance of {balance}.
bdk_err_consent: Confirm that the person gave you this number for texts about this bond.
bdk_err_received_from: Enter who it was received from.
bdk_err_returned_to: Enter who it was returned to.
bdk_err_custom_long: Each custom question can be up to 200 characters.
bdk_err_range: Enter the first and last power number (numbers only, last ≥ first).
bdk_err_range_size: Up to 500 powers at a time.
bdk_err_range_dates: Enter a from and to date (YYYY-MM-DD, from before to).
bdk_status_final: This bond is closed. Its status cannot change.
bdk_deadline_help: Use the deadline on the court notice or set by your state law.
bdk_no_power: No power executed on this bond yet.
bdk_assign_power: Execute a power on this bond
bdk_no_fitting_power: No available, unexpired power with a limit of at least {amount}. Add powers in the inventory.
bdk_checkins_on: The defendant is enrolled in check-ins.
bdk_checkins_enrolled: Enrolled. Send the check-in link from the check-in manager.
bdk_no_forms_yet: Upload your forms in the forms library first.
bdk_counterparts_help: Each signer gets and signs their own copy of each form meant for their role.
bdk_custom_questions: Your own questions (one per line, up to 10)
bdk_custom_ph: e.g. Who will drive the defendant to court?
bdk_deliver_none: Don't send — I'll share the link
bdk_text_cost: Each text costs {cost}, added to your next plan invoice.
bdk_consent_text: The person gave me this phone number for texts about this bond. Texts say "Reply STOP to opt out".
bdk_links_help: These links are shown only now. Copy one to send it yourself or open it on your office tablet. A new link can be made any time (the old one then stops working).
bdk_copy_failed: Could not copy. Select the link and copy it.
bdk_new_link_made: New link made. The old one no longer works.
bdk_resend_by: A new link is sent by:
bdk_void_packet_body: Its links stop working. Signed copies are kept on file.
bdk_download_failed: Could not download the file. Please try again.
bdk_charges_none: Nothing charged yet. Add the premium you agreed on.
bdk_premium_help: Enter the premium your state and surety allow — the app does not compute rates.
bdk_plan_help: The installments must add up to exactly {charged} (all premium and fees). Payments count toward the earliest installment first.
bdk_plan_err_bad_row: Each payment needs a date (YYYY-MM-DD) and an amount above zero.
bdk_plan_err_total: The payments add up to {total}, not {charged}.
bdk_plan_err_order: Two payments have the same date.
bdk_plan_out_of_sync: The plan totals {plan} but the charges are now {charged}. Change the plan to match.
bdk_forms_intro: Upload your own forms (surety forms or your agency forms) as PDFs, say who signs each, and match each fillable field to the case file once.
bdk_storage_off: File storage is not set up on this server, so forms cannot be uploaded yet.
bdk_pdf_rules: PDF up to 10 MB, not password-protected.
bdk_form_uploaded: Form uploaded. Now set who signs it and map its fields.
bdk_form_upload_failed: Could not upload the form. Check that it is a PDF without a password.
bdk_form_no_fields: This PDF has no fillable fields. It will be signed as it is, with the signature page added at the end.
bdk_form_other_fields: {n} checkbox or other field(s) are left as they are.
bdk_signature_fields_help: Map the signature line to "Signature (typed name)" and its date to "Signature date" — they are filled only on the signed copy.
bdk_preview_no_bonds: Add a bond first to preview.
bdk_archive_body: It will no longer be offered for new packets. Packets already sent keep their copy.
bdk_powers_intro: Powers of attorney received from each surety: what is available, executed, voided or returned.
bdk_power_range_help: One power is added for each number from first to last (up to 500). Numbers already on file are skipped.
bdk_return_power_body: Mark it as returned unused to the surety.
bdk_reports_intro: Sums of what you entered, for your sureties and the Department of Insurance. Export any report as CSV.
bdk_rp_liability_help: Open bonds (active and forfeited) by surety.
bdk_rp_surety_help: Powers executed in the date range, with bond amount and premium.
bdk_rp_receivables_help: Bonds with money still owed, and what is overdue.
bdk_rp_receipts_help: Every receipt in the date range. Voided receipts are listed but not counted.
bdk_report_more: {n} more rows in the CSV export.
sgn_link_invalid: This signing link is not valid. It may have been replaced by a newer link.
sgn_ask_agent: Ask your bail agent to send you a new link.
sgn_load_failed: Could not load the paperwork. Check your connection and try again.
sgn_save_failed: Could not save. Please try again.
sgn_questions_help: The agency needs this for the bond application. Fields with * are required.
sgn_uploads_help: Take a photo or choose a file (JPEG, PNG, HEIC or PDF, up to 10 MB).
sgn_selfie_help: Hold your photo ID next to your face so both are clear.
sgn_camera_needed: Camera access is needed to take the photo. Allow it in your settings, or choose a file.
sgn_file_type: Use a JPEG, PNG, HEIC or PDF file.
sgn_upload_failed: Could not upload. Please try again.
sgn_prepare_help: Your copy of each form is filled in with the bond details and your answers. After this, your answers cannot be changed.
sgn_prepare_failed: Could not prepare the documents. Please try again.
sgn_review_help: Open and read every document before you sign. Ask your bail agent about anything you do not understand.
sgn_open_failed: Could not open the document. Please try again.
sgn_esign_consent: Signing electronically: you may ask the agency for paper copies of these documents at no charge, and you may sign on paper instead — to do that, do not sign here and contact the agency (phone above). You can stop at any time before you sign. You need a device that can open PDF files; you will get a copy of everything you sign right after signing. Your typed name is your legal signature (federal ESIGN Act and your state's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act).
sgn_agree_esign: I agree to sign these documents electronically and to receive them electronically.
sgn_agree_terms: I have read the documents and agree to them.
sgn_type_name: Type your full name exactly as shown: {name}
sgn_sign_legal: By selecting Sign, your typed name is applied as your signature on each document, with the date and time.
sgn_sign_failed: Could not sign. Please try again.
sgn_done_body: You signed on {when}. The agency has your signed copies.
sgn_keep_copy: Keep a copy. This link works for 60 days after signing.
sgn_decline: I do not want to sign
sgn_decline_body: The agency will be told you declined. You can tell them why.
sgn_declined_body: {agency} has been told. Contact them if you change your mind.
plan_feat_bond_desk: Bond Desk: your forms filled and e-signed, ID requests, receipts, payment plans, collateral, powers, forfeiture deadlines and reports
plan_feat_checkins: Client check-ins and court reminders — no per-client fee
plan_feat_texts: Texts sent for you: {price} each, added to your plan invoice
bdk_reminder_skipped: Not sent: no phone number or e-mail on file for this person, or texting / e-mail is not set up yet.
bdk_reminder_failed: Not sent: the text or e-mail service refused it. Try again later.
core_unavailable_body: We are focusing on what you need right after an arrest: your rights, help, court reminders and clearing your record. This part comes back once it has been checked.
core_pro_only_body: This tool is for lawyers, public defenders and bail agents. Sign in with a professional account to use it.
gcd_n_week: You have court in one week: {when}.
gcd_n_three_days: You have court in 3 days: {when}. Plan your ride and time off work.
gcd_n_evening: Court is tomorrow: {when}. Set an alarm and get your papers ready.
gcd_n_morning: Court is today: {when}. Leave early. If you cannot make it, call the court or your lawyer before it starts.
gcd_moved: Moved {n} court dates from this phone to your account.
gcd_saved_n: Saved on this phone. {n} reminders set.
gcd_saved_no_reminders: Saved, but notifications are off, so no reminders were set. Turn on notifications in your phone settings.
gcd_saved_web: Saved in this browser. For reminders, use the phone app or create a free account.
gcd_err_past: That date has already passed. If you missed court, see what to do below.
gcd_err_full: This phone already has 20 court dates. Remove an old one first.
gcd_remove_body: Its reminders on this phone will be cancelled.
gcd_title: Save your court date, no account needed
gcd_intro: We remind you on this phone 7 days and 3 days before, the evening before, and the morning of.
gcd_intro_web: Your date is saved in this browser. Reminders need the phone app or a free account.
gcd_account_pitch: Optional: a free account adds text and e-mail reminders, lets family follow your court dates, and keeps them if you lose your phone.
gcd_row_web: Saved in this browser (no reminders on the web)
ckl_share_location: Share my location for this check-in
ckl_location_note: Optional. If you tick it, your location is read once, when you tap Check in now, and sent to {agency} with this check-in only. It is never tracked in the background, and you are asked again each time.
ckl_location_alert_note: If you share your location, {agency} is told when it is far from the address they have for you.
ckl_again_note: You can check in again. It is recorded, but today counts once.
ckl_done: Checked in. Your bail agent has been told.
ckl_done_extra: Check-in recorded. You had already checked in today, so this one is not counted again.
ckl_failed: The check-in was not sent. Check your connection and try again.
ckl_load_failed: The check-in page could not be loaded.
ckl_location_failed: Your location could not be read. Allow location for this page, or untick the box and check in without it.
ckl_link_invalid: This check-in link is not valid. Use the newest text from your bail agent.
ckl_link_expired: This check-in link has expired. Use the newest text from your bail agent, or ask them for a new link.
ckl_stopped: Check-ins are stopped for this link.
ckm_how_5: 5. No smartphone app? Choose "Text link": they get a text with a personal link and check in from any phone browser (5¢ per text).
ckm_channel_app_help: They sign in to the Justice Gavel app with this phone number or e-mail and get push reminders. Free.
ckm_channel_sms_help: No app or account needed: each reminder is a text with a personal link. Texts are {price} each on your plan invoice; check-ins are free.
ckm_consent_text: The person gave me this phone number for texts about their check-ins. Texts say "Reply STOP to opt out".
ckm_err_consent: Confirm that the person gave you this number for texts about their check-ins.
ckm_text_needs_phone: Enter their mobile number to check in by text.
ckm_text_needs_plan: Texts need a paid bail agent plan.
ckm_missed_text_defendant: Text them a reminder with their link the day after a missed check-in
ckm_enrolled_text: {name} is enrolled. Their check-in link was texted.
ckm_enrolled_text_not_sent: {name} is enrolled, but the text could not be sent. Try "Text the link again" later.
ckm_reset_link_body: Every earlier link to {name} stops working, and a new one is texted now.
ckm_text_opted_out: not sent — the number replied STOP
ckm_text_no_plan: not sent — texts need a paid plan
ckm_text_failed: not sent — the carrier refused it
ckm_text_skipped: not sent — texting is not set up yet
ckm_alerts_body: When a check-in day ends without one (in the defendant's time zone), you get a notification and an e-mail.
ckm_alert_phone_needed: Enter your mobile number for alert texts.
ckm_home_help: Set a home point and a radius. When a check-in that shares its location is farther away, you are alerted. Location is only taken at a check-in the person chose to share, never in the background.
ckm_home_radius_bad: Enter a radius from 0.1 to 500 miles.
ckm_home_point_bad: Enter a latitude (-90 to 90) and longitude (-180 to 180), or use a check-in's location.
ckm_outside_radius: Outside the radius: {miles} mi from home
ckm_inside_radius: Within the radius: {miles} mi from home
ckm_extra_checkin: Extra check-in (the day was already done; not counted again)
